routes.description: Establish God as the required transcendent ground of change, contingency, natural order, and objective moral obligation, while defending natural theology as a legitimate inference from observable effects.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the relevant features of reality require an ultimate actual, necessary, intelligent, and moral source; that source is adequately connected to God; and the skeptical alternatives do not remove those explanatory requirements.

motionBridge.description: Connect the cumulative metaphysical, natural-order, and moral inferences to an entity sufficiently characterized as God.

centralBridges.description: Show that change, instrumental causation, or contingency cannot be fully explained without a first actual or necessary foundation.
Show that stable natural regularity or mind-independent intelligible order requires grounding in a directing intellect.
Show that objective moral obligations exist independently of human preference and require a divine intellectual source.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Defend inference from natural effects to an extranatural explanation as methodologically legitimate rather than an appeal to ignorance.
Account for hiddenness, evil, and the interpersonal character of religious knowledge consistently with the proposed divine source.

routes.description: Maintain that belief in God should be withheld unless the affirmative defines and demonstrates a divine being, and show that the offered metaphysical, scientific, moral, and experiential considerations do not meet that burden.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the affirmative inferences remain unsupported, admit nondivine or secular alternatives, or fail to establish the attributes needed for God, making provisional nonbelief the warranted motion-level conclusion.

motionBridge.description: Show that no presented line supplies adequate evidence or a sound inference establishing a sufficiently defined God.

centralBridges.description: Challenge the move from observed change or causation to a timeless first source and from any such source to a divine mind.
Require independent grounds for supernatural explanations and preserve acknowledged ignorance where natural evidence is incomplete.
Show that moral judgment and objective assessment can operate through stated standards, facts, and shared interests without divine grounding.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Require an assessable definition of God and evidence connecting any inferred explanation to the claimed classical divine attributes.
Test private revelation, religious experience, and divine hiddenness against public demonstrability and alternative explanations.

sections.title: Burden of Proof, Definition, and Rational Nonbelief
sections.rationale: This issue fixes what each side must establish, whether atheism is merely withheld belief or a broader position, and how clearly the proposed God must be defined before the existence claim can be accepted.

sections.title: Thomistic Change, Causation, and Necessary Foundation
sections.rationale: The first-mover, causal-regress, and contingency arguments form the principal metaphysical route from ordinary dependent reality to a transcendent foundation, including the disputed transition from that foundation to God.

sections.title: Natural Order and the Method of Extranatural Inference
sections.rationale: This section addresses whether natural regularity, explanatory principles, universals, and cosmological models license inference to an intelligent or extranatural source, and what evidential constraints govern such an inference.

sections.title: Objective Morality and Divine Grounding
sections.rationale: The moral-law dispute is an independent major route to God and turns on the existence and meaning of moral objectivity, the adequacy of secular standards, and whether obligation or altruism indicates a divine intellect.

sections.title: Divine Hiddenness, Religious Knowledge, and Evil
sections.rationale: These issues test whether the proposed God is compatible with persistent nonbelief and suffering, and whether interpersonal or experiential knowledge can provide warranted support beyond publicly demonstrable evidence.

moves.speaker: Michael Egnor
moves.proposition: Change and essentially ordered causal chains require a transcendent actual source, which the argument identifies as God.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly gives Michael Egnor the affirmative opening, and the uninterrupted argument remains in his turn.

response.rationale: This is a constructive presentation of the principal Thomistic argument from change and essentially ordered causal dependence.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it directly develops a principal route from observed change to an actual source.

precisionFindings.rationale: The conclusion is recoverable, but possibilities, causal powers, chains, regress, actuality, and transcendence are compressed together without stable distinctions.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The excerpt asserts that regress is impossible and identifies the required actuality with God without supplying the needed modal and identification bridges.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference is recognizable, but the rejection of infinite regress and transition from an actual source to God remain substantial unsupported bridges.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Observed causal dependence is invoked, but no representative defense establishes that every relevant chain requires the claimed transcendent terminus.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly contacts the indispensable Thomistic-foundation bridge, though its final God-identification remains incomplete.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move presents its own argument and does not meaningfully interpret a live opposing alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The selected excerpt says causal chains lack independent causal ability, rejects an infinite regress of possibilities, and calls the required actuality God.

moves.speaker: Michael Egnor
moves.proposition: The existence of contingent things requires at least one necessary being rather than a reality in which everything depends contingently on something else.
moves.attributionBasis: The argument occurs within Michael Egnor's explicitly introduced and uninterrupted affirmative opening statement.

response.rationale: This constructive move supplies the contingency branch of the central Thomistic foundation rather than answering an earlier opponent.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it clearly advances a central route, although the crucial modal inference is highly compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The necessary-being conclusion is clear, but dependence, contingency, circularity, and necessity are not distinguished with enough precision.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The categorical claim that contingency requires a necessary being exceeds the short assertion about circular dependence and lacks modal qualifications.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The argument moves from individual contingency to a necessary existent, but does not establish why a totality of contingent facts cannot be brute or noncircular.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Examples of contingent persons illustrate the concept but do not warrant the universal explanatory or modal premise needed for the conclusion.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly addresses the central necessary-foundation requirement and is highly relevant within that tier.

representationalCharity.rationale: No developed opposing interpretation is assessed in this constructive statement.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt illustrates contingent existence with the speaker's possible nonexistence, then asserts that everything cannot depend contingently on everything else.

moves.speaker: Michael Egnor
moves.proposition: The stable lawlike behavior of mindless natural objects implies purposeful direction by a mind that knows the ends toward which they act.
moves.attributionBasis: The continuous affirmative opening and first-person framing securely identify Michael Egnor as the speaker.

response.rationale: This constructive move advances the natural-order route by treating stable behavior by mindless objects as purposive direction.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it squarely introduces the intelligent-order thesis but leaves its decisive inference underdeveloped.

precisionFindings.rationale: The proposed inference is identifiable, but pattern, law, purpose, end, and direction by mind are not carefully separated.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Regular behavior is presented as requiring intellect without acknowledging dispositional or structural accounts of natural regularity.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The examples establish regularity, but the transition from mindless regular behavior to purposeful direction by another mind is a substantial non-demonstrated conditional.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Falling rocks and atomic behavior provide examples of regularity, not evidence distinguishing intelligent direction from immanent physical structure.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly contacts the central intelligent-order bridge and states the required conclusion, despite an incomplete warrant.

representationalCharity.rationale: The constructive excerpt does not engage a developed rival interpretation of natural regularity.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt cites falling rocks, atomic behavior, and consistent natural laws while emphasizing that the objects obeying them lack minds.

moves.speaker: Michael Egnor
moves.proposition: Objective moral obligations existing beyond human opinion require a divine intellect and therefore provide evidence that God exists.
moves.attributionBasis: Michael Egnor explicitly introduces this as his tenth proof during his uninterrupted affirmative statement.

response.rationale: This constructive move presents the independent moral-law route from objective right and wrong to a divine intellect.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it directly states both the alleged moral fact and the proposed divine ground.

precisionFindings.rationale: The proposition is clear, but moral objectivity, moral law, existence in a mind, and divine intellect are linked without defining their relations.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Calling the inference very strong evidence overstates an excerpt that does not defend why objective norms must be mental or divine.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The conclusion follows only if objective moral law must exist in an extra-human mind, a decisive premise asserted rather than defended.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The excerpt supplies no independent evidence for objective obligation or comparison with nondivine realist and constructivist grounds.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly addresses the central moral-ground bridge and expressly connects the alleged moral law to God.

representationalCharity.rationale: The constructive argument does not evaluate a specific secular account of moral objectivity.

moves.evidenceBasis: The selected passage says objective right and wrong are beyond human opinion, must exist in a mind outside humanity, and therefore derive from God's mind.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Theistic claims bear the burden of proof, while an undefined or unfalsifiable God cannot rationally be affirmed merely because atheists cannot prove universal nonexistence.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly begins Matt Dillahunty's negative opening immediately before this uninterrupted passage.

components.text: Whether the asserted causal regress requires a transcendent actual source identifiable as God.
Whether contingent existence requires a necessary being rather than another explanatory stopping point.
Whether natural regularity warrants inference to purposeful direction by an intelligent mind.
Whether objective moral obligation requires existence in a divine intellect.

response.rationale: The burden and definition objection is motion-relevant contrary material, but this span does not inspect or defeat the decisive premises of any offered proof.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within relevant nonanswers, it usefully fixes the evidential burden but does not contact the selected proofs' decisive inferences.

precisionFindings.rationale: The burden claim is clear, although saying the burden rests on those saying yes compresses differences between withholding belief and asserting nonexistence.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker acknowledges inability to establish universal nonexistence, but the leprechaun analogy supplies little calibration for specific theistic arguments.

charity.alternative: A theist may offer affirmative natural-theology arguments rather than demand that atheists prove universal nonexistence.
charity.decisiveQualification: Those affirmative arguments still retain the burden of establishing their premises and divine conclusion.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Withholding assent to an inadequately supported or undefined claim coherently follows, with only a bounded ambiguity between weak and strong atheism.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The epistemic principle is defensible, but the excerpt mainly asserts burden placement and uses analogy rather than assessing the supplied evidence.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks completion of the motion-level theistic burden by requiring an assessable and adequately demonstrated God claim.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move fairly preserves the affirmative burden, though it does not yet engage the actual substance of the arguments offered.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt expressly assigns the burden to those affirming God, denies that atheists must prove universal nonexistence, and notes the difficulty of an undefined ontology.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Withholding belief when the available evidence is insufficient is a rational and revisable conclusion consistent with properly placing the burden of proof.
moves.attributionBasis: The passage is continuous with Matt Dillahunty's explicitly assigned negative opening and uses his first-person position.

components.text: Whether the offered metaphysical inference supplies enough evidence to warrant belief in God.
Whether the necessary-being argument overcomes rational and revisable withholding of belief.
Whether the natural-order argument provides evidence sufficient to alter nonbelief.
Whether the moral-law argument provides evidence sufficient to alter nonbelief.

response.rationale: The move explains the rational status of tentative nonbelief but does not analyze any decisive premise or inference in the four earlier affirmative proofs.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within relevant nonanswers, the epistemic framework is clear and issue-bearing but remains nonspecific to the offered proofs.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move clearly describes nonbelief as evidence-sensitive, tentative, and revisable rather than as an incorrigible universal assertion.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The conclusion is expressly tentative and conditioned on available evidence and willingness to change, fitting the stated epistemic warrant.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The relationship among insufficient evidence, involuntary belief, tentative conclusion, proper burden placement, and revision is internally consistent.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The epistemic account is well motivated, but the excerpt does not demonstrate that each affirmative line actually lacks sufficient evidence.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the motion-level skeptical conclusion that assent should be withheld until the affirmative burden is met.

representationalCharity.rationale: This move describes the speaker's epistemic position rather than interpreting a developed opposing alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt states that unsupported claims cannot be accepted and describes nonbelief as tentative, evidence-consistent, and open to alteration.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: If a God interacts detectably or wants and is able to produce belief, that God should be demonstrable; persistent unconvinced nonbelief therefore supports withholding assent.
moves.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted negative opening and explicit first-person account identify Matt Dillahunty as the speaker throughout.

components.text: Whether lawlike natural behavior demonstrates a directing divine mind despite persistent nonbelief.

response.rationale: The hiddenness argument bears on divine detectability but does not answer the natural-order move's premise that regular mindless behavior indicates direction.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within relevant nonanswers, it raises a significant evidential consequence of interactive theism without contacting the selected natural-order inference.

precisionFindings.rationale: The conditional is clear and expressly limited to a God who interacts detectably or wants and can produce belief, though demonstrability admits degrees.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The conditional framing is careful, but remaining unconvinced alone only modestly supports the broader evidential conclusion without additional prevalence evidence.

charity.alternative: God might value noncoercive relationship or permit epistemic distance despite being capable of producing belief.
charity.decisiveQualification: Such aims would need to explain sincere, persistent nonbelief without making every degree of hiddenness compatible with God.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Given its explicit conditions, the inference from capable divine intent to expected belief is coherent, but the evidential strength of one person's nonbelief is limited.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The speaker supplies direct testimony of persistent nonbelief, while broader claims about divine detectability and intent lack representative support.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly contacts the subsidiary hiddenness and revelation bridge rather than the central natural-order inference.

representationalCharity.rationale: The conditional formulation leaves room for different divine aims, though the strongest freedom-based response is not expressly examined.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt conditions its claim on a God who interacts detectably or wants and can convince the speaker, then cites the speaker's continued lack of conviction.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Reports of divine communication do not demonstrate truth when purported messages prove false or harmful and believers preserve the claim by treating every outcome as compatible with God.
moves.attributionBasis: The continuous first-person skeptical presentation and its personal examples identify Dillahunty as the speaker.

components.text: Whether stable natural regularity warrants a directing mind rather than merely reported personal communication.

response.rationale: Criticism of purported messages is pertinent to experiential evidence but does not contact the natural-order argument's decisive regularity-to-intellect inference.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within relevant nonanswers, it provides a concrete reliability criticism but addresses a different evidential channel from its legal target.

precisionFindings.rationale: The reliability complaint is recoverable, but the move shifts from one person's messages to believers generally without an explicit sampling qualification.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker appropriately limits personal knowledge but generalizes from anecdotal cases to a wider believer strategy with limited support.

charity.alternative: Some believers treat alleged messages as fallible interpretations rather than guaranteed divine predictions.
charity.decisiveQualification: That qualification reduces the predictive force such reports can supply as public evidence of divine communication.

logicalCoherence.rationale: False or harmful purported messages and outcome-insensitive interpretation coherently undercut their evidential value, although the generalization is broader than the examples.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: A concrete family example illustrates the concern, but anecdotal and unspecified reports do not establish general unreliability across religious experiences.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It materially supports the subsidiary hiddenness and revelation bridge by challenging the public reliability of claimed messages.

representationalCharity.rationale: The criticism remains relevant under a fallibilist reading, though its win-win description somewhat compresses the range of believer positions.

moves.evidenceBasis: The passage cites reportedly divine messages that were neither impressive nor true and criticizes interpretations under which no outcome counts against God.

moves.speaker: Michael Egnor
moves.proposition: Atheists share a burden of proof because nature allegedly provides evidence of an underlying mind, so both theism and atheism must defend their treatment of that evidence.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator yields the discussion to Egnor, who contrasts Christian belief with Dillahunty's burden-of-proof position.

components.text: Whether only the affirmative theistic claimant bears a burden in this debate.
Whether tentative nonbelief may simply await adequate affirmative evidence without defending a contrary explanation.

response.rationale: The move directly rejects the claimed asymmetry and argues that evidence of mind in nature creates a shared burden, though it does not establish that evidence here.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it contacts the decisive burden claim but leaves the warrant for transferring a positive burden substantially asserted.

precisionFindings.rationale: The shared-burden thesis is clear, but atheism, case, proof, and evidence are used across withholding and positive-denial senses without qualification.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Calling asymmetric burden placement nonsense and claiming massive evidence exceeds the undeveloped support supplied in this selected span.

charity.alternative: Weak atheism may withhold belief without asserting a complete metaphysical explanation of nature.
charity.decisiveQualification: A participant who additionally asserts that no God exists or advances naturalistic explanations can acquire burdens for those positive claims.

logicalCoherence.rationale: A positive atheist claim can carry a burden, but the move infers a shared burden merely from disputed alleged evidence and equivocates over atheism.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The crucial premise of massive evidence for an underlying intellect is asserted without examples or rival comparison in this span.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the motion-level skeptical burden framework by attempting to impose a positive reciprocal burden.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move largely collapses withholding belief into positive metaphysical atheism and omits the decisive distinction between those positions.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says nature contains massive evidence of intellect, rejects the claim that atheists need prove nothing, and declares that both participants must prove their cases.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Observed causal chains within the universe do not demonstrate that equivalent causal relations extend beyond the accessible universe or operate outside time.
moves.attributionBasis: Dillahunty answers Egnor's request to identify Aquinas's second way and immediately supplies the skeptical objection.

components.text: Whether causal relations observed within nature license a necessary transcendent source beyond the accessible universe and temporal domain.
Whether observed dependent existence licenses extrapolation to a necessary being beyond accessible cosmological conditions.

response.rationale: The reply expressly identifies the extrapolation from intracosmic causal chains to inaccessible extra-universal or atemporal conditions and states that the observation does not establish it.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within diagnostic defeats, it explicitly contacts and challenges the decisive scope bridge used by the earlier metaphysical arguments.

precisionFindings.rationale: The scope objection is clear, though beyond the universe, before Planck time, and outside time are compressed into related but distinct limits.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The modest conclusion that observation does not demonstrate extrapolation fits, but the categorical accessibility claim is stated more strongly than defended.

charity.alternative: Aquinas's essentially ordered causation need not be a temporal extrapolation to a state before the universe.
charity.decisiveQualification: The argument still must justify applying its dependence principle universally and show that the terminus is transcendent rather than an immanent structure.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The limitation on extrapolation is sound as a challenge, but references to Planck time do not fully defeat a metaphysical rather than temporal dependence argument.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The contrast between observed internal chains and inaccessible external conditions supports caution, with one material gap concerning the strongest Thomistic formulation.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central causal-gap bridge by disputing the universal extension needed for the transcendent conclusion.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move identifies a real scope problem but partly recasts the Thomistic argument as cosmological and temporal, omitting its strongest non-temporal formulation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt distinguishes causal chains observed within the universe from unobserved causation outside it and invokes limits on investigating the earliest cosmological regime.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Even if a first cause were required, that conclusion neither identifies God nor demonstrates a timeless thinking agent or a mind that created descriptive laws of nature.
moves.attributionBasis: Dillahunty directly rejects Egnor's identification of pure actuality with God and develops several connected skeptical objections.

components.text: Whether an inferred first actual source is sufficiently connected to God and specifically to a timeless thinking agent.
Whether a necessary or foundational being is thereby shown to possess the divine attributes at issue.
Whether descriptive laws of nature require creation by a mind.

response.rationale: The reply expressly isolates the identification gap and states the defeating consequence: even a first cause does not demonstrate a timeless agent or law-creating mind.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within diagnostic defeats, it directly contacts the motion-level identification bridge and several decisive attribute inferences.

precisionFindings.rationale: The concessionary form clearly separates a possible first cause from the further claims that it is timeless, mental, and the creator of natural laws.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The claim is appropriately limited to non-entailment and lack of demonstration rather than asserting that no first cause or divine mind is possible.

charity.alternative: A fuller Thomistic derivation may infer unity, immateriality, intellect, and other attributes from pure actuality.
charity.decisiveQualification: Those further derivations must be presented and defended; the bare first-cause conclusion does not itself contain them.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between existence of a causal terminus and possession of divine mental attributes is explicit, consistent, and defeats the bare identification inference.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conceptual non-entailment is well supported by the missing demonstrations identified, with only a bounded lack of engagement with fuller Thomistic derivations.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the motion bridge connecting the metaphysical terminus and natural order to an entity sufficiently characterized as God.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move fairly grants the first-cause premise for argument's sake and targets the still-required divine-attribute bridge.

moves.evidenceBasis: The selected passage grants discussion of a first cause while emphasizing that no demonstration establishes a timeless thinking agent or mind creating natural laws.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Inference to the best explanation cannot legitimately include a supernatural candidate whose possibility has not been demonstrated merely because an observation lacks a known explanation.
moves.attributionBasis: Dillahunty distinguishes scientific abductive reasoning from Egnor's natural-theology comparison and illustrates the restriction with a dead-body example.

components.text: Whether an undemonstrated intelligent supernatural director may be included as the best explanation of natural regularity.

response.rationale: The move expressly attacks the candidate-admission step in the earlier natural-order inference and explains that unexplained observations do not license undemonstrated supernatural candidates.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within diagnostic defeats, it directly identifies the methodological failure alleged in the best-explanation inference.

precisionFindings.rationale: The methodological proposition is clear, with only an implicit threshold for what counts as demonstrating that an explanatory candidate is possible.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Requiring candidate constraints is sound, but demanding prior demonstration of possibility may be stronger than ordinary abductive practice always permits.

charity.alternative: Abduction can consider novel theoretical entities before direct independent demonstration when they yield explanatory and predictive virtues.
charity.decisiveQualification: A supernatural candidate still needs coherent specification and comparative virtues rather than entry solely from missing explanation.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The restriction blocks arbitrary explanations coherently, though the prior-demonstration requirement is not fully justified for every abductive context.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The dead-body analogy illustrates candidate discipline, but no general account of legitimate candidate generation or supernatural possibility is defended.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central methodological-restraint bridge governing inference from natural effects to supernatural explanation.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move captures the need for constrained comparison but its magic analogy understates legitimate exploratory abduction.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt distinguishes scientific abduction from unrestricted candidate listing and illustrates the point by refusing to add magic to explanations of a dead body.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Ignorance about the Big Bang warrants acknowledging that the answer is unknown, not treating an independently undemonstrated supernatural explanation as plausible gap-filling.
moves.attributionBasis: Dillahunty directly rejects Egnor's characterization of scientific practice and contrasts acknowledged uncertainty with supernatural substitution.

components.text: Whether lack of a known natural account for cosmic origins makes a supernatural causal explanation evidentially plausible.
Whether unanswered cosmological questions independently support a necessary supernatural being.
Whether acknowledged ignorance creates a reciprocal burden to disprove the proposed supernatural explanation.

response.rationale: The move expressly diagnoses the inference from ignorance to supernatural plausibility and states that the warranted consequence is continued acknowledgment of uncertainty.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within diagnostic defeats, it directly contacts the methodological inference and supplies a clear replacement consequence without overextending to impossibility.

precisionFindings.rationale: The speaker clearly distinguishes not knowing an explanation from having positive evidence for a supernatural replacement and limits the claim to current knowledge.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The conclusion is carefully limited: ignorance alone does not raise an independently unsupported supernatural account to plausibility.

charity.alternative: A supernatural hypothesis might gain support from positive features of the evidence rather than merely from an explanatory gap.
charity.decisiveQualification: Those positive features and comparative warrants must be independently stated; ignorance by itself supplies none.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between absence of an explanation and evidence for a particular replacement is explicit and resolves the targeted inferential error.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The epistemic principle is strongly defended by the structure of the inference, with a bounded lack of detailed application to each Thomistic premise.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It is highly relevant within the central methodological-restraint tier and directly blocks an ignorance-based supernatural inference.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move accurately limits its criticism to gap-filling and leaves open genuinely positive or comparative supernatural evidence.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says the cause of the Big Bang is not known and explains that this lack of an answer does not make a supernatural replacement plausible.

moves.speaker: Michael Egnor
moves.proposition: Aquinas's Five Ways are inductive arguments that begin with observations in nature and infer God as their best explanation.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker expressly classifies Aquinas's arguments, contrasts deductive and inductive reasoning, and compares the Five Ways with familiar scientific inferences.

components.text: Whether God may be considered as an abductive explanatory candidate for observed natural effects.
Whether the Five Ways infer from positive observations rather than merely substitute God for ignorance.
Whether inference from observed natural effects illegitimately extrapolates beyond accessible conditions.

response.rationale: The move answers the gap accusation by characterizing the arguments as positive inductions, but it does not establish candidate admissibility or comparative superiority over rivals.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it contacts the decisive methodological objection but supplies analogy and classification more than the needed comparative warrant.

precisionFindings.rationale: The thesis is clear, but induction, abduction, best explanation, God, and supernatural explanation are treated as interchangeable without necessary distinctions.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Equating the Five Ways with successful scientific inference and naming God as best explanation exceeds the analogies and lacks rival comparison.

charity.alternative: The objection permits abduction but requires independently admissible candidates and comparative explanatory virtues.
charity.decisiveQualification: Calling an argument inductive does not itself demonstrate that God is an admissible or superior candidate.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The classification as inductive is intelligible, but analogies to evolution and redshift do not establish the divine conclusion or answer candidate admissibility.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Scientific examples show that induction is used, yet no evidence or comparative criteria establish God as the best explanation of the cited observations.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the subsidiary methodological bridge by defending inference from natural observations to an extranatural explanation.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move answers a stricter rejection of supernatural inference but omits the opponent's decisive candidate and comparison requirements.

moves.evidenceBasis: The selected excerpt classifies all Five Ways as inductive and compares their inference to God with scientific inferences involving evolution and redshift.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Once morality is grounded in the well-being of thinking creatures, objective physical facts can determine whether actions advance or frustrate that stated standard.
moves.attributionBasis: Dillahunty explicitly identifies his situational ethics and proposed moral foundation, then illustrates how objective assessments follow from physical facts.

components.text: Whether objective moral assessment requires a divine intellect rather than a stated secular standard plus physical facts.
Whether atheists lack an accountable alternative treatment of alleged objective moral evidence.

response.rationale: The move directly supplies a secular route to objective assessment, though it does not fully establish that well-being is objectively obligatory rather than a selected standard.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it contacts the divine-necessity inference but leaves the normativity and selection of well-being underdefended.

precisionFindings.rationale: The conditional structure is clear, but morality and well-being are initially described probabilistically and the scope of relevant creatures and interests remains broad.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Objective factual assessment conditional on a well-being standard is well supported, but the move approaches a stronger claim that the standard itself is objectively binding.

charity.alternative: The moral-law argument concerns categorical obligation, not merely factual means to a voluntarily selected goal.
charity.decisiveQualification: A secular account must explain why well-being is normatively authoritative, while the divine account must likewise justify its own normative bridge.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Objective facts can determine means relative to a stated well-being end, but the inference leaves the choice and authority of that end partly unresolved.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The physical-harm example clearly supports objective means-end judgments, with a material gap concerning broader moral obligation and conflicts among interests.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the central secular-morality bridge by presenting a nondivine basis for objective moral assessment.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move offers a serious secular framework but only partially addresses the stronger objection about categorical moral authority.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt proposes thinking-creature well-being as morality's subject and uses the physical harm of decapitation to illustrate objective assessment under that standard.

moves.speaker: Michael Egnor
moves.proposition: Evil is a privation of goodness in finite creation, and God permits suffering for goods including free agency, moral action, and character formation.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator yields the problem-of-evil question to Michael, and the sustained Thomistic and theistic explanation is attributable to Egnor.

response.rationale: This constructive move supplies the affirmative account of evil through privation, finite creation, agency, character formation, and greater goods.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it offers several recognizable compatibility mechanisms but does not develop their necessity or proportional application.

precisionFindings.rationale: The account is recoverable and cautiously framed, though privation, natural evil, free agency, challenge, and character-building cover distinct mechanisms.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker presents the view as a reasonable explanation and acknowledges difficulty, but does not justify its application to the scale and distribution of suffering.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Agency and character formation are possible compatibility explanations, but natural suffering and apparently non-instrumental harms remain material undeveloped scope conditions.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The benefits are asserted as plausible purposes without representative evidence that actual suffering is necessary, proportionate, or reliably productive of those goods.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly contacts the subsidiary objections bridge by offering a direct account of evil and suffering.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move supplies an affirmative theodicy but does not expressly interpret a developed opposing formulation of the problem of evil.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says God permits moral evil for free agency and natural evil as challenge and burden that may build character, while calling the explanation reasonable.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Morality can use an agreed foundation for objective assessments, while appealing to God merely substitutes another disputable foundation and does not solve moral disagreement.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator asks Matt for his favored theistic argument, and Dillahunty's first-person discussion culminates in his established secular moral framework.

response.rationale: This constructive skeptical move argues that secular moral assessment can begin from an agreed foundation and that invoking God does not remove foundational disagreement.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it develops a central skeptical alternative and a direct structural objection to divine grounding.

precisionFindings.rationale: The core parity objection is clear, though foundation, secular morality, disagreement, and solution can concern epistemic, metaphysical, or practical problems.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The categorical claim that God solves no secular moral problem is broader than the demonstrated point that appeal to God does not eliminate disagreement over foundations.

charity.alternative: A divine-foundation theory may aim to ground moral truth metaphysically even if it does not eliminate human disagreement.
charity.decisiveQualification: Such a theory must still establish God's existence, commands or nature, and their normative authority rather than merely name a foundation.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The parity argument coherently shows that naming God does not by itself resolve disagreement, though it does not establish equivalence on every metaphysical question.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The persistence of disagreement among believers supports the practical point, but the universal no-solution claim lacks systematic comparison of divine theories.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the central secular-morality bridge and contests the alleged necessity of a divine moral foundation.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move captures the unresolved epistemic and normative steps but overstates them as defeating every possible metaphysical grounding benefit.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt observes that disagreement persists irrespective of belief and argues that appealing to God merely points to another disputed foundation.

moves.speaker: Michael Egnor
moves.proposition: Atheism is a substantive metaphysical perspective with commitments concerning nature, God's nonexistence, purpose, and moral accountability rather than merely an isolated lack of belief.
moves.attributionBasis: The turn explicitly responds to the preceding characterization of atheism and advances Egnor's recurring claims about atheist metaphysical commitments.

components.text: Whether atheism in this debate is only tentative withholding of belief or a substantive metaphysical position.
Whether atheists avoid positive burdens merely by describing their stance as lack of belief.

response.rationale: The move directly disputes the weak-atheism characterization by attributing naturalistic and normative commitments, but does not show those commitments follow from nonbelief itself.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it contacts the definitional dispute but weakens the target by conflating atheism with additional naturalistic commitments.

precisionFindings.rationale: The proposition is recoverable, but atheism shifts from lack of theistic belief to naturalism, purposelessness, and denial of accountability without scope qualifications.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The categorical attribution of a profound system of associated beliefs to atheists exceeds what follows from atheism alone.

charity.alternative: Atheism can mean only absence of belief in gods, while individual atheists may separately adopt naturalism or positive antitheistic claims.
charity.decisiveQualification: Positive claims of naturalism or God's nonexistence carry burdens, but they are not entailed by bare nonbelief.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The conclusion applies to some positive naturalists, but treating associated beliefs as constitutive of atheism is an unsupported scope expansion.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: No representative evidence establishes that atheists generally affirm nature as fundamental or deny purpose and accountability in the asserted senses.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the motion-level skeptical burden position by arguing that atheism includes affirmative metaphysical commitments.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move acknowledges no distinction between minimal atheism and broader metaphysical naturalism, materially weakening the opponent's stated position.

moves.evidenceBasis: The selected passage attributes to atheism claims about nature's fundamentality, God's nonexistence, lack of ultimate purpose, and lack of ultimate moral accountability.

moves.speaker: Michael Egnor
moves.proposition: Morality by its nature invokes standards outside human opinion, whereas reducing moral judgments to evolved opinions cannot preserve objective wrongness.
moves.attributionBasis: The question is addressed to Michael, and the answer restates Egnor's objective-morality argument through an explicit reductio concerning severe wrongdoing.

components.text: Whether objective moral wrongness can be preserved by factual assessment relative to a human well-being standard.
Whether morality can rest on an agreed human foundation without invoking standards beyond opinion.

response.rationale: The move directly insists that morality claims an extra-opinional standard, but it does not show that the secular well-being framework is merely opinion or that divinity follows.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it contacts the decisive objectivity issue while leaving both the critique of secular grounding and the divine bridge incomplete.

precisionFindings.rationale: The speaker carefully separates whether objective morality exists from whether humans know or access it, making the limited conceptual claim recoverable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The conceptual claim fits ordinary moral discourse reasonably well, but defining morality as objective does not establish objective morality's existence or divine source.

charity.alternative: A secular well-being theory can treat its foundation as intersubjectively selected while deriving objectively true means-end judgments.
charity.decisiveQualification: That yields conditional objectivity but may not establish categorical authority independent of every human evaluative commitment.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between moral truth and access to it is coherent, though the partly definitional argument cannot by itself establish external moral facts.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move offers conceptual reasoning rather than evidence that objective standards exist or that secular well-being accounts reduce to mere evolved opinion.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central secular-morality bridge and supports the need for standards beyond individual preference.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move identifies the strongest remaining normativity issue without denying that secular standards permit some objective factual judgments.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt explicitly says morality, if it exists, is objective and outside mere human opinion while treating human access to it as a separate question.

moves.speaker: Michael Egnor
moves.proposition: Knowledge of God is interpersonal like knowledge within marriage or friendship and therefore may extend beyond scientific testing or publicly demonstrable proof.
moves.attributionBasis: Egnor requests a quick note and describes the Christian relationship with God through personal analogies consistent with his explicitly stated perspective.

components.text: Whether warranted knowledge of God must take the form of publicly demonstrable or scientifically testable evidence.
Whether interpersonal religious experience remains evidentially responsible when alleged communications are false or outcome-insensitive.
Whether interpersonal analogy supplies public evidence meeting the affirmative motion burden.

response.rationale: The move justifies replacing exclusively scientific demonstration with an interpersonal-knowledge standard, preserving the issue of warranted belief, but does not answer reliability or public-burden concerns.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, the justified reframe directly contacts the demonstrability demand but leaves verification and adverse-message evidence unresolved.

precisionFindings.rationale: The interpersonal analogy is clear, though knowledge, proof, relationship, and personal evidence are not distinguished across private warrant and public demonstration.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The modest claim that interpersonal knowledge may include unprovable elements fits the analogy and does not claim the analogy itself proves God.

charity.alternative: The hiddenness objection need not demand laboratory proof; it can ask why sincere seekers lack adequate interpersonal evidence from a capable God.
charity.decisiveQualification: Calling the relationship interpersonal does not explain absent contact or distinguish genuine divine relationship from mistaken interpretation.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The analogy coherently shows that not all personal knowledge is scientific, but it does not establish that a divine relationship exists or is reliably recognized.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Marriage and friendship illustrate non-scientific interpersonal knowledge, yet no evidence connects that ordinary phenomenon to actual knowledge of God.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the subsidiary hiddenness and revelation bridge by reframing the kind of evidence religious relationship may involve.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move fairly challenges an overly scientific demand but only partially addresses the stronger interpersonal version of hiddenness.

moves.evidenceBasis: The selected passage characterizes Christianity as relationship with a person and compares knowledge of God to marriage, love, and close friendship containing unprovable elements.
